sets.concept: A double-t ligature drawn as if it were one extra glyph in Departure Mono: two stems crossed by a single shared crossbar, with the tail on the second t only. I extracted the real Departure Mono 't' from the shipped woff2 (rendered at 128px, quantised back to its design grid) to work from the actual typeface rather than a guess. It is 5x8 units: a 1-unit stem sitting one unit in from the left, a crossbar 1 unit thick placed 2 units down (2 above / 1 bar / 5 below), and a tail that steps right AND turns back up — ".#... / .#... / ##### / .#... / .#... / .#... / .#..# / ..##." — so the brief's hunch was right, the real 't' does step right. Every variant below is built on a strict 2px module (3px in the bolder cut), holds Departure Mono's 2:1:5 bar placement as closely as a 12-row glyph allows, and uses zero accent cells: the accent belongs on the caret in the wordmark, not inside a 16px mark where two coloured cells read as a rendering artifact. All four sit at a centre of mass of y=7.3–7.5 against a geometric centre of 7.5, i.e. optically centred slightly high, which is what a bar-heavy mark needs. I also built and rejected three alternates: a tight 2px counter (stems merge at 16px), an asymmetric 3px crossbar overhang (breaks the 2px module), and a literal transcription of Departure Mono's stepped-and-upturned bowl (its diagonal-only join to the stem reads as a broken tail at one device pixel per cell).

variants.note: Rebuilt on one honest module: every stroke is 2px, the counter between the stems is 4px, the crossbar overhangs exactly 2px on each side, and the tail's 2x2 step terminates on the same column as the crossbar's right end — the original mixed a 1px-thick foot on the left t with a stepped bar on the right, touched the left edge, and left three empty columns on the right; it now sits 12x12 in the 16x16 field with a clean 2px margin all round, with the first t's tail absorbed into the ligature and only the second t keeping its foot, which is what a type designer does and what stops it reading as two letters shoved together.
variants.at16: This is the one that survives at 1:1. Nothing is thinner than two device pixels and the largest counter is four, so there is no moire and no feature that can drop out; the 2x2 foot is the smallest element and it holds. Honest weakness: for the first fraction of a second a stranger reads a wide crossbar over two stems as pi or a torii gate, and it is the bottom-right foot that resolves it into 'tt' — at 16px that resolution is a beat slower than at 32px.

variants.note: Everything steps up to a 3px module — stems, crossbar, and the counter between the stems all 3px, so the rhythm of ink and air stays one-to-one — and the tail grows to a 3x3 step that lands flush with the crossbar's right terminal; the mark fills 14x14 with a 1px margin, which is the correct trade for stickers, a favicon against a busy tab strip, and any place the mark is printed small.
variants.at16: Highest presence of the four at true 16px: it holds the tile rather than floating in it. The real risk is not 16px but 15px or 17px — the 3px counters are the first thing to close up under non-integer scaling or a retina downscale, and when they do the two stems fuse into one slab and the mark reads as a single fat 't'. Use it only where the pixel size is an integer multiple you control.

variants.note: Stripped to the three load-bearing parts — two stems, one shared crossbar, nothing else: the tail goes, the ascender shortens to 2px, and the extra row is spent on the descent so the mass sits where it should; it is the only variant whose horizontal centre of mass lands exactly on 7.50, and at 12x11 with a 3px top margin it has the most air and the calmest silhouette in the set.
variants.at16: Optically the cleanest thing here at 16px — biggest counters, most breathing room, reads as a deliberate glyph rather than a squeezed icon. But removing the tail removes the only cue that distinguishes it from pi, from a torii gate, and from a table/pilcrow symbol, and at 16px there is nothing left to recover the 't' from. It works beside the wordmark, where context supplies the reading; it does not work alone as a standalone avatar.

variants.note: The ligature reversed out of a solid tile — the letterform becomes the negative space and the counter between the stems becomes ink — which flips every relationship in the mark: the crossbar's overhangs now cut into the field instead of projecting from it, and the 2px module is enforced on the white as well as the black (2px knockout strokes, a 2px ink counter between the stems, an even 2px ink border on all four sides, no ink island narrower than 2px and none floating free). It is the version you would actually reach for as an app icon or a GitHub avatar, where a mark on a transparent ground disappears and a tile does not.
variants.at16: It is the only one of the four that cannot get lost — a black tile survives any background, light or dark, and in a tab strip it is the loudest. But it is also the most fragile: at 16px the white counters are exactly 2 device pixels with nothing in reserve, so at any non-integer scale, under any antialiasing, or after a retina downscale the knockouts silt up and the whole thing degrades to a plain black square. It is a fixed-size asset, not a scalable mark, and it should never be the primary logo — only the icon build of it.

sets.verdict: Ship tt-a-refined. It is the only one of the four that is simultaneously legible at 16px, correct as typography, and self-sufficient without the wordmark. C is the more beautiful object — perfectly balanced, more air, the calmest silhouette — and I spent a while wanting it to win, but stripping the tail strips the one feature that makes the shape a letter instead of a symbol, and a logo you have to explain is not reduced, it is broken. B and D are asset builds of A, not competitors: B for stickers and print, D for the app icon and avatar. On whether the concept deserves the identity: yes, but for an unglamorous reason and with a real caveat. The caveat first — a wide horizontal bar over two vertical stems is a shape the eye already owns (pi, a torii gate, a table symbol), and 'tt' is not self-evidently 'terminaltui' to anyone who has not read the name. This mark will never be memorable standing alone; it does not have a shape you could describe over the phone. What it does have is that it is genuinely of the typeface — I checked it against the actual Departure Mono 't' rather than an impression of one, and the proportions, the bar placement and the stepping tail all descend from that glyph — so in a lockup with a Departure Mono wordmark it reads as one system rather than as an icon someone bolted on. For a project at 37 stars whose entire funnel is a GitHub link and a browser tab, a quiet typographic mark that is unmistakable at 16px and unmistakably part of the wordmark is worth more than a distinctive icon that fights the type. That is the correct trade here, and this concept makes it. One thing I deliberately did not do: give both stems a foot. It reads as 'tt' faster and it is more symmetric, and I still think it is wrong — two identical feet is two letters set next to each other, and the whole premise of this mark is that it is one glyph. If the reading speed at 16px turns out to matter more than the typographic argument in real testing, that symmetric version is the fallback, and it is a one-line change to A.

sets.concept: mono-t-baseline — a lowercase 't' whose foot turns and runs right as a rule. The letterform and the command line are one continuous stroke: the vertical is the letter, the horizontal is the line you type on. Refined on a strict 2px module (3px in the bold cut), the rule extends only to the right so it reads as a prompt rather than a symmetrical base, and the accent is a block cursor resting flush at the end of that rule.

variants.note: Held 2px everywhere, lengthened the crossbar to 3-cell arms so it stops reading as a stunted tick against an 8-cell rule (crossbar 8 wide, rule 9 wide — they now rhyme instead of one dwarfing the other), and added a 2x2 accent block flush to the rule's right terminus so the line ends in a cursor rather than a blunt cut; bbox is 12x11 with margins L2/R2/T2/B3, lifting the bottom-heavy rule optically, and the centroid lands at x=7.25 (geometric centre 7.5) so the crossbar's left arm counterweights the rule's rightward pull.
variants.at16: Holds. Every feature is 2 device px, the cursor merges with the rule into a clean stepped terminus rather than floating as dirt, and the counters above and below the crossbar stay open. The 3-cell crossbar arms are the first thing to smear if it is ever scaled to a non-integer size — pin it to 16/32/48px only.

variants.note: Moved the whole system to a 3px module — stem, crossbar, rule and cursor all 3px, and the gap between stem and cursor is also 3px, so one measure governs everything. Crossbar and rule are both 9 wide but offset by 3, which gives the mark a staggered diagonal rhythm the 2px cut cannot afford. The ascender stub above the crossbar shortens to 2 rows, which is what actually happens in bold weights, and the bbox grows to 12x13 with margins T1/B2 to keep the heavy rule sitting high.
variants.at16: Reads as presence rather than detail — 33% coverage, so at 16px it is close to a solid mass with three notches. Every counter is exactly 3px so nothing closes up, but the air is gone. This is the sticker, the tiny favicon and the dark-mode dock icon; it is the wrong cut at 48px and above, where it looks blunt.

variants.note: Same skeleton as A with everything non-load-bearing removed: no cursor, crossbar pulled back to minimal 2-cell arms. Shifted one column right relative to round one because the ink centroid was sitting at x=5.93 — badly left of centre, since the letter is dense and the rule is only two rows; at x=6.93 with margins L3/R2 the mass now reads centred even though the box does not. 44 ink cells, and I could not remove a single one without losing either the letter or the line.
variants.at16: The most legible of the four as a letter, and the emptiest. Nothing breaks — but in a circular avatar crop the left margin is exactly where the crop bites, and the mark reads slightly timid. Worth saying plainly: this is within a few cells of the round-one grid, because that grid was already near the floor for this idea. The reduction confirmed the concept rather than improving it.

variants.note: Inverted the whole idea: a solid 14x14 tile with the t-and-rule reversed out, so the mark is now a screen with a prompt cut into it rather than a letter drawn on paper. Every knocked-out stroke is 2px and every surviving ink band is at least 2px (2 above the stem, 2 below the rule, 2 to the right of the cursor, 3 left of the crossbar). The accent takes the last two cells of the reversed rule instead of sitting beside it, so in monochrome the rule simply shortens and the silhouette survives intact.
variants.at16: This is the honest weak point. All counters are exactly 2 device px, so at a true 16px favicon with any resampling the knockout starts to fill and it degrades toward a dark square with a smudge. At 32px and above it is by far the most recognisable of the four and the only one with real standoff distinctiveness. Ship it as the app icon and avatar at >=32px, never as the 16px favicon.

sets.verdict:
Strongest: **baseline-a-refined**. It is the only one that is simultaneously correct as a letterform (2:5 ascender-to-x-height around the crossbar, symmetric 3-cell arms, uniform 2px), correctly balanced (crossbar's left arm paying for the rule's rightward mass, bottom-heavy form lifted one row), and carrying a second idea beyond "a t" — the cursor waiting at the end of the line. C is the safer favicon and B is the better sticker, but A is the one I would ship.

Now the honest part about the concept. **It is competent and appropriate, but it is not distinctive.** A lowercase 't' with an extended foot is a shape a dozen companies already own; stripped of colour and context it reads about as often as an 'L' or a bracket as it does a 't'. The rationale — letterform and command line are the same stroke — is genuinely good *as a sentence*, and it does not survive the trip into 16 pixels. Nobody looking at the mark will reconstruct it.

That is only a problem if the mark has to carry recognition on its own. Under this brief it does not: §6 is explicit that the identity is the wordmark set in Departure Mono, and the pixel-type-against-neutral-sans contrast *is* the identity. Against that, a quiet, correct, typographically native monogram is exactly the right answer, and a clever, loud symbol would fight the thing it is meant to serve. So: **ship it, as a subordinate monogram — favicon, avatar, package icon — not as a hero symbol.** Do not build a launch animation or a hero lockup around it; it cannot hold that much attention.

One caveat worth acting on: A and D should be treated as a pair, not as competitors. A is the 16px mark; D is the >=32px app icon and social avatar, where the knockout tile gives you actual standoff recognition in a crowded GitHub sidebar. Two cuts of one idea is normal practice and costs nothing here, since D is A reversed out of a square.

sets.concept: cell-void — a solid field of ink with exactly one cell never written. The refinement: the void is no longer a square. It is a *terminal cell* — a portrait rectangle at roughly 2:3 — which is what pulls the mark away from stop-button / die-face territory and ties it to Departure Mono's glyph box. The round-one grid had a 4x4 square void with arms of 3/5/3/5 in both axes, which reads as an unresolved accident rather than a decision; every variant below picks one axis to be asymmetric and holds the other perfectly even. No accent cell appears in any variant: the idea is absence, and putting ink into the void to make it "pop" would destroy the only thing the mark is about. On a colored surface the void takes the background, not the accent.

variants.note: Void changed from 4x4 square to 4x6 portrait (a text cell, not a die pip) and re-centred vertically, so the arms go from an accidental 3/5/3/5 to a deliberate 3 top / 3 bottom / 3 left / 5 right — three equal arms and one wide one, reading as a caret near the start of a written line rather than as a hole punched at random; field held at 12x12 in a 16x16 field for 2px of air on all sides.
variants.at16: One grid cell = one device pixel and no feature is under 3px, so nothing thins out or moires. The 4x6 void is unambiguously taller than wide at 16px — that read survives, which matters because it is the only thing separating this from a generic square-with-hole. The 3/5 left-right imbalance is legible but quiet; at 16px it registers as 'the hole is off to the left', not as an error. Strong dark stamp in a favicon row.

variants.note: Field grown 12x12 to 14x14 with the void held at 4x6, so ink rises from 120 to 172 cells and every arm thickens (4 top/bottom/left, 6 right) — same composition, more mass, for stickers, small dark-on-light chips and any place the mark competes with photography.
variants.at16: Reads as the heaviest and most confident of the set — at 16px it is nearly a solid tile with a slot, which is exactly what you want on a sticker or a 16px tab. The cost is real: only 1px of margin, so any circular or squircle avatar crop will shave the corners and any container that adds its own border will feel choked. Use it where the mark sits on open ground, not inside a rounded chip.

variants.note: Removed the off-centre placement — the only element in variant a that was not load-bearing — leaving 4/4 horizontal and 3/3 vertical arms and perfectly even negative space; what is left is the irreducible statement of the concept, ink plus one cell-shaped absence, nothing steering the eye.
variants.at16: The cleanest of the four at 16px: symmetrical, evenly countered, no ambiguity about whether the imbalance is intentional. That is also its whole problem. With the asymmetry gone, the portrait proportion of the void is doing 100% of the differentiating work, and at 16px the delta between a 4x6 hole and a 4x4 hole is two rows of pixels. Half the audience will file it as a frame, a stop button, or the 'no signal' block.

variants.note: Abandoned the square field entirely: the outer shape is now itself a terminal cell (10 wide x 14 tall) containing a self-similar void at the same proportion — a cell inside a cell — with the counter lifted one row (3 above, 5 below) because a mathematically centred counter in a tall block always sits optically low.
variants.at16: The most specific of the set and the only one nobody will mistake for a stop button — a portrait block with a portrait counter reads as a glyph, which is precisely right next to a Departure Mono wordmark. The honest cost: it is 10px wide in a 16px box, so in a row of square favicons it looks smaller and less authoritative than its neighbours, and in a circular avatar the 3px side margins become 3px of wasted arc. It is a letterform, not an icon.

sets.verdict:
Strongest: **void-a-refined**. It is the only variant that is both unmistakably deliberate and shaped like an icon. The portrait void gives it a reason to exist beyond geometry, the 3/3/3/5 arm rhythm makes the asymmetry read as a decision rather than a slip, and 12x12 in a 16x16 field is the correct amount of air for an avatar. It is the version I would ship, with b as the sticker/small-size cut and d reserved for use immediately beside the wordmark, where its glyph-ness is an asset rather than a liability.

But I do not think this concept deserves to be the identity, and I would rather say so than defend my assignment. A filled square with a rectangular hole is one of the most occupied shapes in graphic design — stop button, record frame, Bauhaus poster, the 'no signal' block, half the die faces, an 'O' set in any grotesk. Everything I have done here is damage control on that fact. The portrait proportion of the void is the only differentiator, and it is a two-pixel-row distinction at the size where a favicon actually lives. Test it the way marks get tested: nobody can draw this from memory and nobody can describe it over the phone in a way that distinguishes it from ten other marks. It has no retellable story.

What it is genuinely good at: it is quiet, it never breaks, it scales from 16px to a billboard without adjustment, and it sits politely beside a Departure Mono wordmark without competing. If the brief is 'we need a favicon and an avatar so the wordmark is not alone', void-a does that job at a professional standard today. If the brief is 'we need a mark that can eventually carry the brand without the wordmark' — a GitHub avatar people recognise in a feed — this concept will not get there, and no further refinement will fix it, because the weakness is in the premise rather than the execution. In that case the right move is to spend the next round on a concept with a specific referent (the cursor and the line it is on, the page-route relationship, the cell grid as a structure rather than as a bitten square) and keep void-a in the drawer as the safe fallback.

sets.concept: flow-branch — the file-tree connector from a `pages/` directory listing: a vertical spine with arms whose reach increases downward, so the arm tips form a stepped diagonal. Refined here on a strict 2px module with a 2-2-2-2-2-2 vertical rhythm; the accent, where present, marks the last arm's tip as "the page you're on".

variants.note: Held every stroke at 2px and put the whole mark on one 2-unit vertical rhythm (stub 2 / bar 2 / gap 2 / bar 2 / gap 2 / bar 2 = 12 rows), so both counters are identical and the arms and the spine share a weight. Added a 2-row spine stub above the first arm — it says this branch hangs off a parent, which is what a pages/ subtree actually looks like, and it is also what fixes the vertical balance: mass centroid lands at row 7.63 against a 7.50 target, versus 8.17 for the original bottom-anchored version. Shifted the spine one column right of geometric centre (cols 4-5, bbox margins L4/R2) because a tree is intrinsically left-heavy; that puts the ink centroid at col 7.03 instead of 6.03. Arm widths step 6 / 8 / 10, an even 2-cell increment, and the last arm terminates the spine as a proper └.
variants.at16: Reads correctly and stays clean — every feature is 2 device pixels, nothing moires. The weakness is the diagonal: a 2px step between arm tips is present but quiet, so at exactly 16px it can read as a comb rather than a stepped tree. The accent is 2×2 device pixels; it registers as a colour tick, not as a shape, and if the favicon is ever downscaled below 16 it is the first thing to vanish. Silhouette without the accent is unchanged and still balanced.

variants.note: Same composition at 3px stroke with 2px counters — dropped the spine stub because a 3-rhythm version of it would run 18 rows and not fit the field. Vertical placement is exact: centroid row 7.65 on rows 1-13. Horizontally I let it sit at cols 3-13 (centroid col 6.74, 0.76 left of true) rather than push it right, because at this density the mark reads as one block and a 1-column right margin would look clipped on a sticker die-line. Counters are thinner than the strokes here (2 vs 3), which is a deliberate trade: it buys presence and keeps the negative space even between the two gaps.
variants.at16: Too dense for a 16px favicon — the 2px counters close up optically against 3px bars and the three arms start to merge into a filled wedge. This is a sticker, screen-print, and dark-mode-avatar mark at 32px and up, where the heavier stroke reads as confidence instead of mud. The stepped diagonal survives better than in variant a because there is more mass to step.

variants.note: Stripped the accent and the spine stub — neither is load-bearing — and spent the saved space on the one thing that is: the step. Arm widths now go 4 / 7 / 10, a 3-cell increment instead of 2, so the diagonal is unmistakable rather than inferred. Ten rows on a 2-2-2-2-2 rhythm, 10 columns wide, and the balance lands almost exactly: centroid row 7.46, col 6.96. Note the margins are T2/B4 — the mark deliberately sits high because all ten cells of its widest bar are on the bottom two rows; even bbox margins would read as sinking.
variants.at16: The best of the four at this size. Every gap is 2 device pixels, every step is 3, nothing to lose and nothing to smear. It survives a dark background and it survives being the 16px tab icon next to eight other tabs, which is the actual test. No accent means no colour dependency and no silhouette question — what you see is the whole mark.

variants.note: Same concept, dissolved spine. Instead of one vertical trunk with arms hanging off it, the trunk becomes short risers and the mark is a descending staircase: three 5-wide treads, two 2-wide risers, all 2px. This is indentation itself — what nesting looks like in a file listing — rather than the tree glyph that ships in half the dev tooling on npm. It reads as depth and forward motion instead of hierarchy-at-rest, it is the only one of the four whose silhouette is not left-anchored, and it centres perfectly without a fudge: centroid row 7.50, col 8.00. Accent stays on the final tread's tip, the current page, and is the only place the eye stops.
variants.at16: Holds up well — 2px throughout, treads and risers all read, and the descent is obvious at a glance. The honest risk is semantic, not optical: stripped of the trunk it can be misread as a generic list/indent/align icon rather than a routing tree, especially at 16px where you have no context. It is the more ownable form and the less legible idea; those trade against each other.

sets.verdict:
Strongest of the four: **branch-c-reduced**. It is the only one where the concept's whole payload — a spine, three arms, an increasing reach — survives intact at 16 device pixels with nothing left to cut. The 3-cell step makes the diagonal read as intent rather than accident, the counters are dead even, the optical lift off the baseline is correct for a mark this bottom-loaded, and dropping the accent removes the one element that was never going to survive a favicon anyway. Ship c as the favicon and small-size lockup, a as the primary mark wherever the accent is large enough to carry brand colour (32px+, README header, the site nav at 2x), b for stickers and print. They are the same drawing at three densities, which is what a system looks like.

On whether the concept deserves the identity: semantically, yes — this is the only one of the round-one ideas that says the actual thing the product does. `pages/about.ts → /about` is the pitch, and this is a picture of it. But I want to be plain about the cost. The tree connector is the single most-used glyph in developer tooling; it is in build-tool logos, monorepo tools, tree-sitter, half the CLI READMEs on GitHub. Craft can make this version *good* — I think a and c are genuinely well-built — but craft cannot make it *ownable*. A stranger will read "some dev tool" instantly and "terminaltui specifically" never. That is a real weakness for a project whose whole job right now is to be remembered by someone comparing four frameworks in one afternoon.

The escape hatch is d. The staircase keeps the meaning (nesting, routing, depth) while abandoning the glyph everyone else uses, and it is the only mark in this set I have not seen before. It trades a little instant legibility for actual distinctiveness. If the decision criterion is "reads correctly with zero ambiguity", take c. If it is "still recognisable in twelve months among competitors", take d and let the wordmark do the explaining — that is what Departure Mono is there for. What I would not do is ship the round-one grid: its mixed rhythm and 12-cell bottom bar made it sit low and read as a bracket, and that is the version that would have looked accidental.

sets.concept: frame-nested-brackets — concentric L-brackets. Structure containing structure: routes containing pages containing layouts. Refined against a strict 2px module (2px stroke, 2px counter) so every stroke and every gap is the same width, and optically nudged down-right to compensate for the form's inherent top-left mass. The round-one grid had a real defect: its vertical gaps were 1px while its horizontal gaps were 2px, and its three bars terminated at three different columns (14, 13, 14). Both are fixed here. All four variants are verified: zero 1-cell ink or gap runs anywhere inside the bounding box, and mass centroids within 0.33 of the field centre.
sets.verdict:
Strongest is nest-d-reinterpreted, and it is not close. It is the only variant with true 180-degree rotational symmetry, so its centroid lands on 7.50/7.50 exactly with no fudging — it will never look "slightly off" in an avatar circle. It is the lightest (25% coverage) yet the most legible, because the two brackets are separated by an even 2px diagonal channel instead of three parallel bars competing for the same 16 rows. And it reads as a viewport, not a staircase.

That last point is my honest reservation about the concept as briefed. The concentric same-direction stack (a, b, c) has a specific failure mode nobody named in round one: at 16px, "long bar, medium bar, short bar, each with a descender" is the universal icon vocabulary for a bar chart, a settings/sliders glyph, or a "steps" indicator. Squint at nest-b and it is a chart. That ambiguity is fatal for a mark that has to survive as a 16px favicon next to twenty other tabs. Nesting-as-staircase is architectural in the abstract and generic in practice.

nest-d fixes it by rotating the second bracket 180 degrees. Two opposed corner brackets embracing an open field is unmistakably a frame — and a frame is what a framework is. It also happens to look like a terminal viewport with the chrome stripped off, and it echoes the bracket pair `[ ]`, which sits naturally beside a monospaced pixel wordmark. It is the only one of the four I would put on the repo.

So: the concept survives, but only in its rotated form. Ship nest-d. Keep nest-a as the conservative fallback if the team wants three levels of nesting for the narrative — it is correctly built and I would not be embarrassed by it, but it is a competent generic icon where d is a specific one. I would drop nest-b entirely: at 53% coverage with 3px strokes against 2px counters it is the loudest and the most chart-like, and boldness is not what this brand is selling. Departure Mono is precise, not shouty; the mark should match. If you need a sticker version, scale nest-d and let the white space do the work.

One process note: nest-c is the only variant where I had to choose between bounding-box centring and mass centring, because its bottom-right quadrant is genuinely open rather than enclosed by a third level. I chose mass (T3/B1 margins) — an open counter is not read as part of the form the way an enclosed one is. That asymmetry looks wrong when you inspect the grid as text and looks right when you render it. Worth knowing before someone "fixes" it.

variants.note: Same three-level nest, rebuilt on a strict 2px module: every stroke is 2px and every counter is 2px, where the original mixed 1px vertical gaps with 2px horizontal ones. All three bars now terminate on the same column (14) instead of 14/13/14, and all three stems drop to the same row. Nudged one cell down-right (margins T2 B1 L2 R1) because the form's mass is inherently top-left — that single-cell shift moves the centroid from 6.83 to 7.47 against a field centre of 7.50, and it also gives the heaviest element, the long outer bar, the extra air it needs. Diagonally symmetric about the main axis. Accent is the innermost L only (17% of filled cells): outer structure is the framework, the innermost element is your content.
variants.at16: Holds cleanly — 96 filled cells, no 1px features anywhere, so nothing moires. The three 2px counters read as three distinct levels. The honest risk is semantic, not technical: at this size a descending stack of bars with descenders is close to the universal bar-chart / sliders glyph, and some viewers will read it that way before they read 'nesting'. Flatten the accent to solid ink at favicon size; a 2px mint stripe sandwiched between 2px ink stems vibrates on a low-DPI display, and the silhouette loses nothing without it.

variants.note: Strokes go to a uniform 3px against 2px counters, which forces the nest down to two brackets — three levels of 3px will not fit in 16 cells with survivable gaps. The third level becomes a solid 4x4 core block instead of a third bracket, which is what buys the balance: that block anchors the bottom-right corner and pulls the centroid to 7.18 with no positional nudge needed, where the light versions need one. Fills the full 14x14 with 1px margins, which is correct for a sticker and deliberate. Accent is the solid core (12% of filled).
variants.at16: Very loud — 53% ink coverage. It survives, because the 2px counters still resolve at one device pixel each, but it reads as a solid black quadrant with two notches cut out rather than as three nested things. It is the strongest of the four on a die-cut sticker or embroidered on a cap, and the weakest as a favicon: it is also the variant most likely to be misread as a bar chart, because the 3px bars are the dominant feature. Do not use it below about 32px.

variants.note: Two brackets, not three. The third level was doing narrative work, not visual work — with it gone the two remaining counters are large and unambiguously equal, and coverage drops from 38% to 28%. Nothing else changed: same 2px module, same terminations, same diagonal symmetry. Because the bottom-right quadrant is now genuinely open rather than enclosed by a third bracket, the counter no longer reads as part of the mark, so I centred on mass rather than on the bounding box: margins are T3 B1 L3 R1, which looks lopsided as text and lands the centroid at 7.39. No accent — there is nothing left to accent.

One stroke system throughout: gutter = 2 cells everywhere, no 1px anything, clean square silhouette (the raggedness lives in the internal splits, not the outline), accent = the focused pane, always the smallest pane, always under 15%.

variants.at16: Reads as a solid square cut by two 2px gutters that step across each other — legible, the offset survives, the accent pane reads as one distinct chip in the lower right. The only cost is a 1-cell outer margin, thinner than the internal gutter, so it sits close to the edge of an avatar circle; it does not clip, but it is at the top of the size range.

Best at 32px and above, where the four rectangles resolve as rectangles.

sets.verdict:
Strongest: tiling-a-refined. It is the only one that keeps the meaning (four panes, one gutter, splits that refuse to align, one focused pane) while being provably deliberate — point symmetry means no viewer can read the offset as sloppiness — and it survives an avatar crop, which b does not. Ship a; keep b as the sticker/square-tile lockup; c is the prettiest object but has stopped saying anything; d is the best idea and the riskiest mark.

On the concept itself, plainly: this is the most crowded corner of software iconography. Every tiling WM, every IDE layout toggle, every "split view" button, every grid icon in every UI kit is rectangles-with-gutters. Misalignment is a real differentiator conceptually, but at 16px the differentiator is a 6-row offset — a detail — sitting on top of a form that a stranger has already seen a hundred times. It resolves to "layout icon". It does not say terminal, it does not say framework, and it has no relationship to Departure Mono's letterforms, which the brief says *is* the identity. Its one genuine merit is that it encodes something true and specific about the product: pages laid into panes, with one focused — that maps to file-based routing better than any glyph would.

My honest recommendation: if terminaltui has exactly one mark, it should come from the typeface — a block cursor, a prompt, a caret — because that is where the brand's distinctiveness actually lives, and the pixel grid is already the identity's whole argument. This concept is competent, well-crafted in variant a, and I would not be embarrassed to ship it. But it is a good execution of a generic idea, and I would rather say that than defend my assignment.

sets.concept: A sphere whose terminator — the light/dark boundary — is rendered as a coarse dither: the mark is a picture of the framework's own image algorithm. The refinement moves the dither from single pixels (which turned to grey mush) up to 2×2 blocks, and — critically — puts a solid 2px limb around the whole circle so the silhouette never depends on the dither surviving. The dither now lives strictly inside a closed circular outline, as a 50% checkerboard of 2×2 blocks laid on a 5-row block grid that is mirror-symmetric about the optical centre line. Every feature in every variant is 2px minimum; there is not a single 1px stroke, gap or counter in the set. Rendered/verified sheets: /private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-omar-Desktop-Projects-TUI/1d34d0e1-9f78-439b-b2f1-8343f33b21f6/scratchpad/final2-light.png and final2-dark.png

The round-1 grid let the dither eat the circle's edge, which is why it read as a golf ball; here the silhouette is structurally independent of the dither. All seven counters are identical 2x2 squares, so the negative space is perfectly even, and horizontal centre of mass lands at 7.09 against a field centre of 7.5 — the slight leftward bias is the correct optical compensation for a mark whose right side is half-tone.
variants.at16: The circle is unambiguous and there is no mush — but be honest about what survives: the 50% checker optically averages, so at 16px you read 'dark circle with a lighter zone right of centre', not 'dithering'. The idea becomes visible around 24px and is fully legible at 32px+. Secondary risk at 16px: it can read as a coin or a button.

variants.note: Same interior geometry, but the disc grows to a full 16px and the limb thickens from 2px to 3px — 180 ink cells against A's 136. Deliberately fills the frame: for stickers and for tiny UI where a 1px margin just evaporates.

Trade-off is real: zero margin, so any circular avatar crop will shave the limb, and the dither is even more likely to read as flat grey than in A. Use it where the mark sits on its own, not inside a rounded container.

variants.note: Stripped to three tones instead of two: solid dark side, a two-block-wide checker fringe, and a genuinely empty lit side held only by the limb. Removing the outer checker column is what makes it work — the light side is now actually light, so the terminator reads as a boundary between two states rather than as a texture patch. The fringe is the minimum that still reads as a dither and not a staircase: three tabs attached to the dark mass plus two detached 2x2 islands.
variants.at16: The best small-size read in the set among the circles, because it carries the idea with tonal contrast rather than texture — a moon phase with a bitten edge. The three tabs stay individually visible where A's checker greys out. Cost: at 130 ink cells with a mostly-empty right side, mass sits well left (COM 6.89); the closed limb keeps the circle reading as the object, but it is the least balanced of the four.

variants.note: Figure and ground inverted, and the sphere moved inside a terminal cell. The mark is now a 14px square — the cell — with the lit sphere as negative space, its terminator dissolving right into a two-column checker. Same concept (the mark is a picture of its own algorithm) but it says the other half of the story: an image, quantised, living inside one cell. The accent is a single isolated 2x2 ink island at the exact centre — the one sampled pixel. Silhouette test passes trivially: strip the accent and you still have a square with a clean counter.
variants.at16: The most legible of all four by a clear margin. A square silhouette does not soften under downscaling the way a circle does, the large white counter gives real contrast, and the checker blocks stay individually readable because they sit against a big empty field rather than against more ink. The accent survives as one distinct coloured pixel. Weakness: it is the furthest from a sphere, and a black square with a white shape inside is a crowded formal space — it reads closer to a generic app icon than the circles do.

sets.verdict:
Strongest is C. It is the only circle in the set that carries the idea by tonal contrast rather than by texture, which is why it works for the same reason at 16px, 32px and 128px instead of degrading into a different mark at each size. It also states the concept most clearly: dark side, quantised boundary, lit side. A is the fullest and most correct expression of the concept and is what I would ship if the mark mostly appears at 24px+; B is a straight utility variant of A; D is the best pure mark in the set but has drifted furthest from the sphere.

On whether the concept deserves the identity — the honest answer is a qualified yes, and the qualification matters more than the yes.

What I fixed: the round-1 grid failed because the dither was doing two jobs, describing the shading AND defining the silhouette. Moving to 2x2 blocks and giving the circle an unbroken 2px limb separates those jobs, and it kills the golf-ball read completely. There is no mush left in any of these four.

What I could not fix: a 50% checkerboard is, optically, grey. That is not a craft failure, it is what dithering IS — the technique works by averaging. So at 16px the thing that makes this concept special is invisible; you get a competent circle with a lighter zone. Everything special about it only switches on around 24px. I also hit a hard geometric ceiling worth recording: a 12px disc with a 2px limb has room for exactly three 2x2 dither blocks, and three blocks in checker offset read as a chevron, not as a dither. That is why every variant here is 14px or 16px. And a diagonal terminator cannot carry a block checkerboard at all — anti-diagonals have constant parity, so the pattern collapses. The dither has to run against a vertical boundary.

So: this concept can be the identity if the system uses the mark at 24px or larger in most placements and treats the dither as a system element in its own right — section rules, hero field, loading states — rather than asking a 16px favicon to carry it. If the requirement is that the concept itself must be legible at favicon size, this idea cannot deliver that, and a simpler mark should win. That is a real constraint on the brand, not a detail, and it should be decided deliberately rather than discovered after launch.
